explanation: Fires on the final subword piece that completes a multi-token word or name, often a technical term, a proper name or a code identifier (benzophen|one, Khron|os, CIRCU|IT, naltrex|one, E-select|in, __esModule). Whole common words and function words give only weak activation.

Fires inside non-English text (French, German, Portuguese, Russian, Japanese, Finnish, Tagalog), on verbs, auxiliaries, particles and word-internal subword pieces, most strongly in grammatical or verb positions. Code tokens and LaTeX tokens give weak to moderate activation.

Mixed. It fires strongly on ' id' after an HTML tag name (<ul id, <li id), on ')' closing a news-wire dateline like '(Reuters)', on ' (@' in tweet citations, on 'critically ill', on 'ANOVA', and on the second word of fixed multiword names (American League, per share). There is no single shared feature.

Fires on a word that is ungrammatical, redundant or oddly placed for the context: a duplicated word ('is there there'), 'an well', 'stop of course', 'I changes', 'behalf on'. It also fires on tokens following non-native or awkward phrasing ('is going to', 'was going to'). Fluent text gives only weak activation.

Diffuse. It fires on many unrelated tokens: word-internal pieces of names (Mogoll|on, Murre|ll, DO|OH), 'help'/'helps', 'of' in 'because of', 'about'/'almost' before numbers, '.BUTTON' in code. No common context is apparent.

Fires on structural tokens in formal or technical headers: digits and hyphens in legal docket numbers ('No. 93-3005'), the start of academic abstracts, keyword separators, and Go or Ruby type and method tokens ('*FmtCtx', '.new'). It also fires on conjunctions and punctuation in lists in scientific prose. Overall it looks like a mixture of formal-document scaffolding.

Fires on the first digit of a four-digit year, '1' in 1xxx, or '9' in 19xx when tokenized as '1|9|90'. The strongest cases are directly after 'in' in founding or first-description phrases ('founded in 1954', 'first described in 1946') and in birth-date parentheses. Years in other positions, such as lists or legal dates, give moderate activation.

Fires on the second token of a fixed compound or multiword term, where the token completes a known phrase ('Air pollution', 'liquid crystal', 'External links', 'described above', 'Classification of Disease', 'Titanium silicide', 'braced ourselves'). Weaker on generic continuations. The examples are fairly heterogeneous.

Fires on an opening parenthesis ' (' that starts a parenthetical aside or definition after a noun phrase. The strongest cases are license boilerplate ('documentation files (the "Software")', 'DAMAGES (INCLUDING', 'License (the "License")') and prose asides ('ten patients (nine men'). It is moderate before abbreviations or statistics in scientific text, and near zero on other tokens.

Two strong patterns: 'yards' in American-football stat lines ('172 yards', 'receiving yards') and other football terms ('tackles', 'starts'), and ' to' in patent openings ('The present invention relates to'). There is also scattered weaker firing on scientific and technical terms.

Fires on distinctive content nouns and named entities that carry a topical or cultural meaning, especially in espionage, politics and entertainment contexts ('undercover', 'bipartisan', 'boycotted', 'Bollywood', 'Taliban', 'Billboard', 'sitcom', 'heterozygous'). Function words and generic tokens give weak activation.

Fires on mixed tokens in news, legal and technical boilerplate: digits in timestamps ('Updated: Mar 22, 2019 14:36'), the closing quote after a quoted reply ('Absolutely,"'), 'way of example', 'Elin's', citation digits, and the period after a taxonomic family name. No unifying theme.

Fires on ' and' or ',' (sometimes ' or') that joins a noun phrase to a following coordinate item or clause, right after a concrete noun phrase ('the DLLs and', 'a bunch of bread,', 'license agreement,'). It is weaker on other connectives like 'than' or 'with'.

Fires on a token right after the subject or modal of a clause in formal prose, where an adverb or verb modifying the predicate begins ('to effectively buy', 'Obesity adversely affects', 'which partially explains', 'have significantly eroded', 'could further'). It also fires on the start of surname tokens like 'Van' and 'Yan'. The core job is pre-verbal adverb or predicate onset, with name offshoots.

Fires on a content noun or adjective that is one item in a list or a coordinated series of policy, health or product categories ('for retirement, disability', 'walnuts, almonds and', 'calories and fat', 'size, weight or power', 'National Rifle Association'). Its role as a list element in descriptive or policy prose matters most.

Fires on sports and physical-exercise vocabulary: yoga poses, burpees, free-kick, submission, rock climbing, shot put, backstroke, gymnastics. Strongest on fitness or exercise terms, moderate on general sports terms (ring, track, circuit), near zero elsewhere.

Fires mostly on ' of' or ' no' in quantifier or idiomatic constructions ('most of them', 'any of us', 'by no means', 'of no fault', 'in no way', 'all of whom'). It also fires on scattered other tokens ('am' in 'I am unaware', 'then', 'although'). The quantifier/idiom 'of'/'no' is the main job.
Heterogeneous. It fires on 'IS' in 'AS IS', the last piece of names (Sakharov, Banksy, OneWeb), 'to form', 'polyQ', 'Vitamin E', code identifiers and others. There is no evident shared property.

Fires mostly in German, Spanish and Portuguese text, on function words and word-internal pieces ('bei der', 'oder', 'gegen die', 'logrado', 'para'). It also fires on a few English or code tokens, such as 'The function' and 'QsciLexer'. The main job is non-English (especially German) text.

Fires strongly on ' to' in the MIT-style license phrase 'persons to whom ... are furnished to do so', and on '.' after 'Boost Software License, Version 1.0'. Other license-boilerplate punctuation is moderate. It also fires on scattered prepositions and nouns in ordinary prose ('in four games', 'services'). License boilerplate is the main job.

Fires on a middle subword fragment of a long word that has been split into odd pieces, often because of soft hyphens or letter spacing, or because it is non-English or Latinate ('Av|anz|ados', 'med|itat|ion', 'exempl|ified', 'ult|imat|ely', 'O P I N I O N', 'benachteil|igt'). It is weak on whole words.
